claim: For every screen, design the empty, loading, success, and error variants alongside the populated one; treat the populated view as one of five deliverables, not the deliverable.
why: Real users encounter these states constantly — first login, slow networks, failed requests — so a design that only covers the ideal case leaves the majority of real moments undesigned.
when: Any screen whose content depends on user data, remote fetches, or an action that can succeed or fail.

claim: Build an empty state from three parts: a visual anchor (illustration or small animation), a sentence explaining why the space is empty, and a primary button that performs the action that would fill it.
why: A blank region gives the user no model of what the screen is for; the message supplies the model and the button removes the guesswork about what to do next.
when: First-run dashboards, lists, and collections that a new account starts with zero of.

claim: When the user triggers an asynchronous action, show a loading indicator during the wait and always resolve it into an explicit success or error message — never let the indicator simply disappear.
why: An unresolved action forces the user to infer the outcome from the absence of feedback, which is the moment they lose confidence in the system.
when: Third-party integrations, connections, deploys, saves, uploads — anything with a round trip long enough to notice.

claim: Deliver the outcome of a long-running background job as a push notification or persistent status surface rather than only inline on the screen that started it.
why: The user typically navigates away while the job runs, so feedback bound to the originating view will be missed.
when: Builds, deploys, imports, exports, batch processing — anything that outlives the user's attention on one screen.
fails: Short, immediate actions, where a notification is heavier than the inline confirmation the user is already looking at.

claim: Judge state design by whether it keeps the user informed and in control, not by whether it looks finished — use that as the acceptance test for each state you add.
why: States are product decisions about the user's mental model of what the system is doing, so polish alone does not tell you whether the state is doing its job.
when: Reviewing or critiquing screens before handoff.

claim: Audit an existing product for missing states by walking each entry point — sidebar items, integration flows, list views — and asking what the screen shows with no data, mid-request, on success, and on failure.
why: Missing states are invisible when you look at a finished mockup; enumerating them per-surface is what makes the gaps show up.
when: Adding product-thinking to an interface that was designed visually first.

claim: Give every tappable or clickable control a visible state change that fires on press, before any resulting navigation or data work completes.
why: Users judge whether their input registered by what the screen does immediately; with no local change, a delay reads as a dead control and provokes repeat taps.
when: Any button, link, icon, or row that triggers an action whose result is not instantaneous.
fails: The state change is so heavy or slow it becomes its own delay; on genuinely instant transitions the pressed state can flash and read as a glitch.

claim: Scale the feedback to the expected wait: a pressed/disabled state for sub-second work, an explicit loading indicator once the wait becomes perceptible.
why: A momentary state change answers 'did it register'; a longer wait raises a different question — 'is it still working' — which only a persistent indicator answers.
when: Actions with variable or network-dependent latency, such as screen transitions, saves, and submissions.
fails: Showing a spinner for near-instant work adds perceived slowness and visual noise.

claim: Disable or visually deactivate a control while its action is in flight so it cannot be triggered twice.
why: An unacknowledged control invites repeat presses, which can duplicate the action; greying it out both signals progress and blocks the duplicate.
when: Submits, saves, purchases, and navigation that kicks off a request.
fails: Long-running actions where the user legitimately needs to cancel or back out — the control must then offer an escape, not just lock.

claim: When an action moves an item somewhere else in the product, update the destination too — badge the tab, section, or list that now holds it, not only the control that was pressed.
why: Changing only the control confirms the tap but not the outcome; users are left guessing where the thing went and whether anything was actually stored.
when: Save, bookmark, add-to-cart, add-to-collection, and similar actions whose result lives in a different part of the navigation.
fails: Persistent badges that never clear train users to ignore them; the indicator should resolve once the destination is visited.

claim: Treat the filled/active icon state as the first layer of feedback, not the complete answer — pair the state toggle with a cue that communicates the consequence.
why: Icon fill communicates a binary toggle; it carries no information about where the result went or that a collection has grown.
when: Icon-only toggles like save, favourite, follow, and like.
fails: Trivial toggles with no downstream destination, where an extra cue is redundant clutter.

claim: Audit interactive feedback in both directions — remove decorative effects that carry no meaning, and add missing ones wherever an action currently produces no immediate visible change.
why: Over-animation and dead controls are the same underlying failure: the amount of motion in the UI is not matched to the amount of information the user needs.
when: Reviewing a prototype or build for interaction polish.

claim: Keep dashboard motion functional and short — use it to clarify state or reveal data, not to decorate; save expressive animation for marketing pages.
why: Dashboards are tools people use repeatedly all day; flourish that delights once becomes friction on the hundredth view, and it competes with the data for attention.
when: Designing transitions, hovers, and loading states in internal tools, admin panels, and analytics dashboards.
fails: A landing page, product tour, or onboarding moment where expressive motion is doing persuasion work rather than interface work.

claim: Charts are the one dashboard surface where you can spend extra interaction budget — give each data mark a hover state that reveals precise information the static view omits.
why: A chart necessarily compresses data to a shape; hover is how the user recovers exact numbers without cluttering the default render.
when: Any chart where the static rendering cannot label every point without becoming noisy.
fails: Touch-only contexts, where hover does not exist and the information must be reachable by tap or shown persistently.

claim: On hover, surface both the raw value and a derived comparison (percent change, share of total) rather than the number alone.
why: The raw figure answers 'how much'; the derived figure answers 'is that good', which is the question a dashboard reader actually has.
when: Time-series and metric charts where a point is only meaningful relative to a prior period or a whole.
fails: Data with no meaningful baseline or denominator, where a percentage would be arbitrary.

claim: For multi-series or multi-bar charts, isolate the hovered element by dimming the others instead of only highlighting the target.
why: Reducing the visual weight of everything else creates far more contrast than brightening one item, and it keeps the dimmed context visible for comparison.
when: Bar charts, grouped series, and legends where many marks compete at equal visual weight.
fails: Charts with only two or three marks, where dimming is more distracting than the ambiguity it resolves.

claim: Apply optimistic UI to actions that almost always succeed: update the interface immediately on click, fire the server request in the background, and only reconcile if it fails.
why: Round-trip latency shows up as an awkward dead pause between intent and result; assuming success removes the pause entirely and makes the app feel fast without making it faster.
when: High-frequency, low-stakes, reversible actions — delete, archive, toggle, star, reorder, mark-as-read.
fails: Actions that are irreversible, financially consequential, or genuinely likely to fail validation (payments, submissions with server-side rules), where a false confirmation is worse than a wait.

claim: Pair every optimistic update with a rollback path: if the request fails, restore the prior state and tell the user what happened.
why: Optimism is a bet; without a visible correction, a failed request silently leaves the UI lying about the data.
when: Any optimistically-applied mutation.

claim: Judge dashboard interaction by perceived speed, not measured latency — spend design effort on removing waiting states before optimising the backend.
why: Users report a dashboard as fast or slow based on the gap between their action and visible feedback, which front-end technique can close independently of server time.
when: Prioritising performance work on data-heavy internal tools.
fails: When the underlying operation is slow enough that faking completion produces long-lived incorrect state.

claim: When surfacing a behavioural statistic about the user, pair the raw number with a neutral frame or comparison rather than presenting it bare; a naked count reads as an accusation.
why: Users supply their own interpretation of an unlabelled number, and for anything with moral weight attached (time spent, money spent, skipped workouts) that interpretation defaults to guilt.
when: Digital-wellbeing summaries, usage recaps, spending reports, activity streak breaks — any surface that reflects a user's own behaviour back at them.
fails: Contexts where the user explicitly asked for a hard number as an accountability tool and softening it undermines the feature they opted into.

claim: Never make a monetary upgrade the only way to turn off a notification the product itself initiated; always offer a free, permanent 'don't show this again' path.
why: Coupling relief from an interruption to payment converts the interruption into leverage, so the user reads every future instance of it as a shakedown rather than a service.
when: Any recurring interstitial, banner, or reminder that has a paid tier which removes it.
fails: Ad slots in an explicitly ad-supported free tier, where the exchange is the stated deal and users already understand the contract.

claim: Design wellbeing and self-control features as opt-in, and only trigger them for users who have set a limit themselves.
why: The same message is help when requested and judgement when unsolicited; consent is what separates the two, and the interface cannot tell which user it is talking to unless it asks first.
when: Screen-time limits, usage nudges, 'take a break' prompts, and any feature that assumes the user's current behaviour is a problem.
fails: Legally mandated disclosures or genuine safety interventions, where opt-in defeats the purpose.

claim: Time interruptions to task boundaries, not to arbitrary counters — never break into a session at its most relaxed, low-intent moment.
why: An interruption's cost is set by what it interrupts; the same modal that is tolerable between tasks feels like an intrusion mid-leisure, and the resulting irritation attaches to the product, not the message.
when: Any modal, full-screen takeover, or blocking prompt in a continuous-consumption interface (feeds, video, games, music).
fails: Genuinely urgent interruptions — security alerts, unsaved-data warnings, payment failures — where delay costs more than annoyance.

claim: Test critical copy by reading it aloud in the persona of an already-irritated user; if it can be heard as a rebuke, rewrite it.
why: Copy drafted with helpful intent is silently read in a helpful tone by its author, but users bring their own tone, and the harsher reading is the one that determines the emotional outcome.
when: Reviewing notification, empty-state, error, and upsell copy before ship.

claim: Trigger behavioural-nudge overlays on an accumulated-session-time threshold rather than on page count, page load, or entry — measure how long the user has actually been in the flow and only interrupt once that crosses a limit.
why: The behaviour being addressed is duration-shaped ('an exorbitant amount of time'), so the trigger must measure the same thing the message calls out; anything else fires on users who aren't doing the thing.
when: Designing self-regulation prompts, screen-time nudges, or 'are you still there' interventions in browse-heavy or feed-style interfaces
fails: The long session is the intended, valuable use — research tools, comparison shopping with a genuine purchase intent, or media playback — where a duration trigger punishes engaged users

claim: Give an interruption a concrete alternative action rather than only telling the user to stop; the modal should offer the substitute behaviour as its primary button.
why: A bare 'you've been here too long' leaves the user with nowhere to go but back into the flow they were in, so the only executable option is dismissal; naming a replacement gives the dismissal a destination.
when: Any nudge that asks a user to break an in-progress habit loop
fails: The suggested alternative is transparently self-serving for the product, which reframes the intervention as an upsell and burns the trust the nudge depends on

claim: Write nudge copy in a teasing, second-person voice that names the specific behaviour, instead of neutral system language — the personality is what makes an unrequested interruption land as a joke rather than a scold.
why: An overlay the user never asked for is an imposition; humour is the toll it pays for the interruption, and specificity ('you've been here this long') proves the product actually noticed rather than firing a generic timer.
when: Consumer products, low-stakes self-improvement prompts, and any interruption where the user's compliance is entirely optional
fails: The message carries real consequences (billing, security, data loss) or the audience is in a vulnerable state — compulsive spending, addiction — where mockery reads as contempt

claim: Scope an intervention to the tail of the usage distribution: define the threshold so it fires only for the small group whose behaviour is actually a problem, not for the median user who does a milder version of the same thing.
why: The pitch explicitly distinguishes 'we've all done it a little' from 'some people are worse' and targets only the latter, which keeps the interruption rare enough to stay meaningful.
when: Designing any interruption whose value depends on scarcity, where firing too often trains the user to dismiss it reflexively
fails: You lack the telemetry to place the threshold honestly and end up guessing, catching normal users with a message written for extreme ones

claim: Never block a user's core task on the platform, browser, or device they arrived with; degrade features gracefully instead of denying entry.
why: A hard block at the point of intent converts a product into an obstacle — the user has an urgent goal and the interface substitutes a company's distribution agenda for it.
when: Designing entry points for tools people depend on: mail, docs, storage, banking, anything with time-sensitive or obligatory use.
fails: A genuine technical capability is missing (an unsupported codec, API, or security requirement) — then a clear, specific explanation plus a fallback path is legitimate, not a dark pattern.

claim: Do not put an unskippable timed ad between a user and functionality they already have access to; monetise around the task, never inside the doorway to it.
why: Charging attention as a toll makes the interface feel extractive rather than useful, and the resentment lands on the product, not the advertiser.
when: Any ad-supported or freemium surface where the paywalled action is something the user considers baseline.
fails: The gated thing is genuinely premium and the user has an obvious free alternative — a rewarded-ad unlock for optional extras reads as a fair trade rather than a hostage situation.

claim: Treat an 'alternative path' as real only if it restores the user's original goal at comparable cost; if the only alternative is worse in time, dignity, or effort, it is a coercion mechanic, not a choice.
why: Offering one bad option and calling it an option is the structural signature of a dark pattern — the interface simulates consent while the outcome was predetermined.
when: Reviewing any consent dialog, upgrade prompt, or compatibility wall that presents two or more buttons.
fails: Both paths genuinely serve the user and differ only in preference; the test is cost symmetry, not the mere presence of two buttons.

claim: When you must interrupt with a blocking state, write it as a diagnosis with a fix, not as an announcement of company strategy — say what is wrong and what the user can do in one screen.
why: The parody's message explains the vendor's motives rather than solving the user's problem, which is exactly what makes it read as hostile.
when: Writing error, unsupported-browser, and access-denied screens.

claim: Test hostile design ideas by prototyping them against a high-stakes user moment; if the mock-up produces visceral anger in seconds, the pattern is unshippable regardless of its business case.
why: The bit works because it stages the block during an urgent, emotionally loaded task — the same staging makes an effective internal check on coercive flows.
when: Evaluating growth-driven or monetisation-driven interruptions before they reach production.
fails: The chosen scenario is unrepresentative — staging an edge case as if it were typical will over-reject reasonable friction.

claim: When reporting progress against a goal, express the remaining gap in the smallest realistic unit of effort the user can act on today (e.g. 'about a 25-minute walk'), not in an aggregate that reads as impossible.
why: Mathematically identical shortfalls feel motivating or hopeless depending on the unit chosen; an impossible-sounding framing tells the user to quit rather than act.
when: Any progress-tracking, streak, budget, or quota UI that surfaces how far behind the user is.
fails: The gap genuinely cannot be closed — then a soft reset or reframed goal is more honest than a false 'you can still do it'.

claim: Do not have the product compute and volunteer the user's failure; surface shortfall only where the user has gone looking for it, or pair it with a next action.
why: An unprompted push notification arrives without consent and turns a passive check-in into a judgement, which erodes trust in the app's voice.
when: Push notifications, in-app modals, and interstitials triggered by falling behind rather than by user action.
fails: Genuinely time-critical alerts (medication, deadlines, security) where interrupting is the point.

claim: Write product copy in a neutral, factual register; if a line would read as sarcastic or scolding when the user is already having a bad day, cut it.
why: The narrator draws the line himself — humour aimed at the user reads as passive aggression, and one more clause tips it into open hostility. Copy has no tone of voice to soften it and will be read at the user's worst moment.
when: All error states, failure states, and shortfall messaging.
fails: Products with an established, opt-in irreverent brand voice — and even then, only on non-failure surfaces.

claim: Never offer an action whose presence implies the user has failed — a 'lower your goal' button shown at the moment of shortfall is an accusation dressed as a control.
why: Affordances carry meaning by placement; suggesting an escape hatch exactly when the user is behind reads as the product concluding they can't do it.
when: Any secondary CTA placed inside a failure, shortfall, or downgrade context.
fails: Settings the user has navigated to deliberately, where goal adjustment is a neutral, expected control.

claim: Keep goal editing in settings, not in progress notifications — put the destination for the action where the user's intent originates, not where the system's judgement lands.
why: Placing a control next to a negative state binds the two together and gives the control a connotation it wouldn't carry elsewhere.
when: Deciding where to surface configuration controls relative to status messaging.

claim: Test failure-state copy by reading it aloud as if spoken by a person to the user's face; if it sounds rude, rewrite it.
why: The chapter's whole method is to make interface tone audible — copy that seems fine in a spec reveals its attitude when voiced.
when: Reviewing microcopy for notifications, empty states, and errors.

claim: When a modal blocks the user from continuing, put the instructions for escaping or disabling the block inside that modal itself, not buried in a settings page.
why: A blocking state removes the user's ability to go looking for the off switch; the moment they are trapped is exactly when they need to know the exit exists.
when: Any interrupt, hard gate, or required-field modal that halts the primary task flow

claim: Any opt-in constraint or strict mode must ship with a visible, reversible way to turn it back off, discoverable from inside the constrained state.
why: Users adopt strict modes optimistically and often want out after real usage; if the reversal is hidden, the feature feels like a trap rather than a tool.
when: Focus modes, lint-style enforcement, discipline features, and any setting that adds friction to a routine action
fails: Constraints that exist for safety, compliance, or data integrity, where an easy self-serve off switch defeats the point

claim: Do not let a design's intended tone — playful, strict, hostile, minimal — become an excuse to skip baseline usability work like clear exits and explanatory copy.
why: Tone is a layer on top of the interaction; the underlying contract of orienting the user and letting them recover still applies regardless of how the product feels.
when: Opinionated, gamified, or deliberately friction-heavy products

claim: To force a naming or labelling habit, leave the field genuinely empty rather than pre-filling a generic default.
why: A default like 'Frame 42' reads as already-complete, so nothing signals the user to change it; an empty value is a visible gap that invites input and can be validated against.
when: Systems where meaningful user-authored names matter downstream — layers, files, branches, variables, saved views
fails: High-volume creation flows where naming every object is disproportionate to its value and an empty state just becomes noise

claim: Trigger required-input validation at the moment the user tries to leave the object, not while they are still working inside it.
why: Deferring the prompt to the point of departure preserves the user's flow during creation and makes the interruption read as a consequence of their own action rather than a random nag.
when: Required fields on newly created objects in a direct-manipulation canvas or editor
fails: When leaving is itself the intent — e.g. abandoning or deleting a draft — where the gate should not fire at all

claim: Do not place a payment or account-creation gate in front of content a user needs to complete a short, immediate, real-world task; let them finish the task first and ask for signup afterward.
why: The friction cost of a gate is judged against the size of the job it interrupts — a subscription prompt reads as extortionate when it stands between someone and cooking dinner tonight.
when: Utility content consumed in a single sitting under time pressure: recipes, how-to steps, transit directions, product manuals, unit conversions.
fails: The content is the entire commercial product — a paid course, an original reporting operation, or a professional tool where the gate is the business model rather than an add-on tax.

claim: Before importing a monetisation or conversion pattern from another category, check whether that pattern is tolerated there or merely endured; do not copy widely-hated mechanics just because they are widespread.
why: Ubiquity is not validation — the narration treats article paywalls as already maddening in their native context, so replicating them elsewhere multiplies an existing failure instead of borrowing a proven one.
when: Choosing gates, interstitials, cookie flows, or signup walls by benchmarking competitors and adjacent industries.

claim: Never stack two conversion demands in the same blocking moment — force a choice between paying and registering, not both, since each gate independently costs a large share of users.
why: Presenting payment and account creation together compounds the perceived cost of a small task and reads as greed rather than as a value exchange.
when: Designing any access wall, trial flow, or download gate.

claim: Use anticipated user anger as an explicit design check: name the emotion the flow will produce and, if it is anger rather than mild friction, redesign the gate instead of tuning its copy.
why: The segment evaluates the change purely by how furious it would make a real person, which is a faster and more honest signal than conversion-rate reasoning alone.
when: Reviewing flows that interrupt a user mid-goal — walls, upsells, forced onboarding.
fails: Used as the only metric; some necessary friction (destructive-action confirmations, security checks) rightly annoys users and should stay.

claim: Gate any pairing or device-control handshake behind an explicit, owner-initiated confirmation on the owner's device; never let proximity alone grant control.
why: Control over physical actuators is irreversible in the moment — a light flicked off or a lock opened cannot be undone by an undo button — so the cost of a wrong grant is borne in the real world, not the UI.
when: Designing onboarding, sharing, or guest-access flows for IoT and smart home products where the app commands physical hardware.
fails: Ephemeral, low-stakes shared contexts the owner has deliberately opened up — a conference room display or a party speaker queue — where friction on every join outweighs the harm of a stranger's input.

claim: Scale the strength of a permission gate to the physical consequence of the action, so lights and locks do not sit behind the same access tier.
why: The narration treats a stranger toggling a bulb as annoying but a stranger touching a lock as catastrophic; a single flat permission model prices both the same and therefore prices the dangerous one wrong.
when: A product surface exposes a mixed inventory of devices with wildly different failure costs under one list or one sharing toggle.

claim: Do not ship a risky capability enabled by default on the reasoning that users can disable it in settings; default it off and let users opt in.
why: Buried settings are discovered only after harm occurs, so a default-on switch effectively means the risky state is the shipped state for most users.
when: Any feature whose worst case affects the user's safety, privacy, or physical property.

claim: When a device changes state without the user having touched it, surface who or what triggered it and offer an immediate revoke, rather than letting the state change appear anonymous.
why: The opening moment of confusion — watching something toggle with no explanation — is itself the design failure; unattributed state changes leave the user unable to act on the problem.
when: Multi-user or automation-driven systems where an entity other than the current viewer can mutate shared state.
fails: Routine background automations the user authored themselves, where per-event attribution becomes noise.

claim: Encode relatedness by drawing a shared container (background fill, border, or card) around the items that belong together; items outside the container read as a separate group.
why: Enclosure is read pre-attentively as a grouping cue, so a single boundary does the work that a heading or explanatory copy would otherwise have to do.
when: A row or cluster of peer items where some subset forms a unit — segmented controls, filter chips, toolbar sections, related form fields.
fails: Everything is boxed, or containers nest several layers deep — once enclosure is the default, it stops signalling anything and just adds visual noise.

claim: Show which option in a set is currently chosen by giving exactly one item a distinct container treatment (filled pill, raised surface) while its siblings stay unstyled.
why: A single item styled differently from its neighbours reads as 'this one is the current state', and the untouched siblings read as available alternatives, which also communicates that the control is switchable.
when: Mutually exclusive choice among visible options: tabs, segmented controls, toggle groups, nav items.
fails: More than one item carries the selected treatment, or the same fill is also used for hover/focus — the viewer can no longer tell selection from transient feedback.

claim: Communicate that a control is unavailable by lowering the contrast of its label and icon (grey it down) rather than by hiding it or explaining the restriction in text.
why: Reduced contrast reads as reduced capability, so users stop expecting a response from it before they click and don't need an error message afterwards.
when: A control that exists in the layout but cannot act right now — unmet prerequisites, insufficient permissions, an empty selection.
fails: The dimmed styling drops below legibility for low-vision users, or the same muted grey is also used for ordinary secondary text — then 'quiet' and 'disabled' become indistinguishable.

claim: Before writing helper text or an instructional tooltip, try to make the visual treatment carry the meaning; reach for words only when no styling cue can express it.
why: Perceptual cues are decoded instantly and language-independently, while instructional copy costs the user a read and often goes unread entirely.
when: Any interaction whose availability, grouping, or current state needs to be conveyed.
fails: The concept is genuinely arbitrary — pricing rules, data provenance, destructive consequences — where visual styling can hint at severity but cannot convey the specifics.

claim: Give every interactive element a visible response for each of its states — resting, hover, pressed, selected, disabled — so the element declares its own interactivity.
why: An element that never changes appearance gives the user no evidence it can be acted on; the state changes are what make its capability visible.
when: Buttons, nav items, links, list rows, cards, and any custom control built from generic markup.
fails: Touch-primary contexts where hover never fires — pressed and selected states must carry the load there instead.

claim: Reserve tooltips for naming an already-visible affordance (typically an icon-only control), not for teaching an interaction the visual design failed to signal.
why: A tooltip is hidden until hovered, so anything essential placed inside it is invisible to users who never hover and to touch users entirely.
when: Icon-only toolbar buttons and dense controls where a persistent label doesn't fit.
fails: The interaction itself is non-obvious — a tooltip cannot rescue a control that gives no indication it is clickable in the first place.

claim: Assign one visual property per meaning — enclosure for grouping, fill for selection, contrast level for availability — and don't overload a single property with two jobs.
why: The demo layers three different messages onto the same three items without collision precisely because each message rides a separate visual channel; reusing a channel makes the messages ambiguous.
when: Designing a component's state matrix or a design system's interaction tokens.

claim: Design and ship at least four visual states for every button: default, hover, active/pressed, and disabled — treat a button with only a default style as incomplete.
why: Each state answers a different user question — is this clickable, am I about to click it, did my click register, is it available right now — and omitting one leaves that question unanswered.
when: Any clickable control in a UI: primary and secondary buttons, icon buttons, links styled as buttons.
fails: Touch-only interfaces where hover cannot occur; there the hover state is dead weight and effort should shift to a stronger pressed state and larger hit target.

claim: Add a fifth loading state with an inline spinner to any button that triggers an asynchronous operation, and disable further presses while it runs.
why: Without it the user has no evidence the action started and will press repeatedly, firing duplicate requests.
when: Submit, save, purchase, or any control that kicks off a network request or long computation.
fails: Operations that resolve near-instantly, where a flashing spinner reads as a glitch rather than progress.

claim: Give text inputs a distinct focus state that changes the border or adds a ring the moment the field receives keyboard or click focus.
why: Focus is the user's positional anchor in a form; without a visible marker they cannot tell where typing will land, especially when navigating by keyboard.
when: All form fields, selects, textareas, and custom input widgets.

claim: Pair an input's error state with both a colour change on the border and an adjacent message that names the problem — never colour alone.
why: The border colour signals that something is wrong; only the message tells the user what to change, and colour-blind or low-vision users may miss the border entirely.
when: Validation failures on form fields at submit or on blur.

claim: Reserve a separate warning state, visually distinct from error, for issues that are advisory rather than blocking.
why: Collapsing soft advisories into the error style trains users to ignore red, and blocks submission for problems that should not block it.
when: Optional-field problems, weak-but-acceptable passwords, unusual-but-valid values.
fails: Simple forms where every rule is hard-blocking — an extra tier just adds ambiguity about whether the user may proceed.

claim: Show a loading indicator for any data fetch that has not resolved, so the interface never presents an empty or static region while work is in flight.
why: An unchanged screen is indistinguishable from a broken one; the indicator converts perceived failure into perceived progress.
when: Page loads, list refreshes, search results, and any content region populated from a remote source.

claim: Confirm completed actions with an explicit success message rather than relying on the absence of an error.
why: Users need positive evidence the operation finished; silence after a submit leaves them uncertain whether to retry.
when: Saves, submissions, deletions, and any action whose result is not immediately visible in the layout.

claim: Attach small motion responses to continuous gestures such as scroll and swipe so the interface tracks the user's input in real time.
why: Direct-manipulation gestures feel broken when the surface does not move with the finger; micro-animation supplies the physical response the gesture implies.
when: Touch surfaces, pull-to-refresh, swipe-to-dismiss, scroll-linked reveals.
fails: Overuse across every element, which turns feedback into visual noise and slows perceived responsiveness.

claim: Audit every interactive element by asking what the user sees at each stage — before, during, and after the action — and design a state for any stage that currently shows nothing.
why: Missing feedback is a gap that is invisible in a static mockup; only walking the interaction timeline surfaces it.
when: Component design reviews and pre-handoff QA of any interface.

claim: For any action whose result is invisible (copy, save, add to cart, subscribe), fire a short confirmation animation after the action resolves — hover and pressed states alone are not sufficient.
why: Hover and active states only prove the control received input; they say nothing about whether the underlying operation succeeded, so an invisible outcome leaves the user guessing and re-clicking.
when: The effect of a button lives off-screen or outside the UI — clipboard writes, background saves, network requests, state changes with no visible surface.
fails: The result is already plainly visible on screen (a row appears, a field fills in); adding a redundant confirmation there is noise.

claim: Treat interaction states and outcome confirmation as two separate layers you must design independently: states cover hover/press/focus/disabled, confirmation covers success/failure after the fact.
why: The chapter shows a button that is fully specced at the state layer and still fails the user, which means state coverage cannot substitute for outcome feedback.
when: Speccing any interactive control in a design system or component library.

claim: Deliver the confirmation as a small transient element that enters with motion — a chip, toast, or label sliding into view — rather than a static swap or a blocking dialog.
why: Movement draws the eye to the new information without stealing focus, and a lightweight transient element confirms without interrupting the task.
when: Confirming low-stakes, reversible, successful actions.
fails: Destructive or high-consequence outcomes, or errors that need acknowledgement — those warrant persistent or blocking feedback instead.

claim: Anchor the confirmation near the control that triggered it so the cause-effect link is unambiguous.
why: In the demo the chip appears at the copy button, tying the feedback to the specific action; feedback placed far from its trigger forces the user to infer what it refers to.
when: A screen has multiple actionable controls that could each produce feedback.
fails: Global or system-level events (connection lost, sync complete) that belong in a consistent app-level region.

claim: Choose the micro-interaction's tone deliberately along a practical-to-playful axis, and let brand and stakes set the dial rather than defaulting to decoration.
why: The same mechanism serves both pure utility and personality, so the expressive choice is a separate decision from the functional requirement.
when: Designing repeated or signature interactions where brand character can show through.
fails: High-frequency utility actions, where playful flourishes become tiresome or slow the user down.

claim: Budget for the invisible layer: when you design any dense component, enumerate its hover, focus, active, empty, loading, error, selected, and overflow states before calling it done, and expect that inventory to be roughly as large as the visible design.
why: Almost all of a component's actual functionality lives in states that aren't on screen at rest; a design that only covers the resting state is a picture of an interface, not a working one.
when: Designing data-dense components — tables, lists, grids, boards — or reviewing a dashboard that looks finished but feels thin in use.
fails: Static or single-purpose surfaces (a marketing hero, a printed report) where no interaction states exist to design.

claim: Put row- and cell-level actions behind hover rather than rendering them permanently: reveal a copy chip, edit button, or action menu inside the cell on hover instead of adding a dedicated actions column.
why: Dense tables have no spare horizontal room; hover-revealed controls give every cell its own action surface without spending layout width or adding visual noise to the resting state.
when: Per-row or per-cell operations in a table where columns are already competing for width.
fails: Touch-primary interfaces, where hover doesn't exist — those actions need a persistent target, a long-press, or a swipe instead. Also fails for destructive or rarely-discovered actions that need to be visible to be trusted.

claim: Signal hidden content with a small persistent marker rather than hiding it entirely — e.g. a tiny corner triangle on a cell that carries a comment, which expands on interaction.
why: Content that is fully hidden is undiscoverable; a low-cost glyph makes it findable while costing almost no space or attention in the resting state.
when: Any per-item metadata — comments, notes, attachments, validation warnings — attached to a subset of cells or rows.
fails: When most items carry the marker, at which point the indicator becomes noise and the data should be promoted to a real column.

claim: Add a tooltip to every icon-only control and every label whose meaning isn't self-evident, including abbreviated column headers and computed metrics.
why: You cannot assume the user reads an icon the way you do, and ambiguous labels are the point at which people either guess or stop; a tooltip carries the extra detail without spending layout space.
when: Dashboards and admin tools, which concentrate icon-only actions and jargon-heavy metric labels.
fails: Touch-only contexts where hover tooltips never fire, and cases where the tooltip is being used to paper over a label that should simply be rewritten to be clear.

claim: Before creating a new page for a feature, first try to express it as a state, overlay, or panel inside an existing surface — a drawer, modal, popover, or inline expansion.
why: Once you account for hidden UI, most new functionality already has a home in the current layout; a dedicated page adds navigation cost and fragments a flow that could have stayed in place.
when: Adding functionality to an established product where the relevant context already lives on a screen the user is on.
fails: Genuinely deep or multi-step workflows, or anything that needs to be linkable, bookmarkable, and shareable — those earn their own route.

claim: Design the low-frequency screens too — feature announcements, onboarding explainers, first-run empty states — even though a given user may see them once or never.
why: Their rarity is exactly why they get skipped, and their absence is what makes a build read as unfinished; they also carry disproportionate weight because they land at the moment of first contact.
when: Taking a product from prototype to something real users are onboarded into.

claim: Treat the orchestration of hidden UI — what triggers each state, what it displaces, how states stack and dismiss — as a separate design problem from the visual detailing of the pieces themselves.
why: Sizing and spacing an individual chip or tooltip is mechanical; deciding the trigger rules, priority, and dismissal behaviour when several hidden layers can coexist is where the real difficulty and most of the bugs live.
when: Any component with more than one hidden affordance — e.g. a cell that can be hovered, commented on, selected, and edited.

claim: Apply hidden-state accounting at every scale, not just to large containers: a single cell deserves the same state inventory as a drawer or a modal.
why: Small elements are assumed to be trivial and so get skipped, but in a dense layout they are repeated hundreds of times, which multiplies any missing state into a pervasive gap.
when: Reviewing component libraries or design specs where large surfaces are documented and atoms are not.

claim: Treat the 404 page as a designated personality slot: give it a custom illustration, joke, or small interaction rather than shipping the framework's default error text.
why: The user landing there has already hit a dead end, so nothing productive is being interrupted — the expectation is low and the memorability payoff is high.
when: Any site or product with a public error route, especially when the rest of the interface must stay restrained and functional.
fails: On error states that block active work — failed checkout, lost form data, auth failure — where the user needs a clear recovery path and levity reads as tone-deaf.

claim: Escalate error-page interactivity to match the effort you can sustain: static custom illustration at minimum, an interactive element next, a playable moment that returns the user to a working page only when you can maintain it.
why: The cited examples sit on a clear ladder — illustration, quiz, snake game with auto-redirect — showing that the concept scales rather than being all-or-nothing.
when: Deciding how much to invest in a low-traffic delight surface.
fails: When the interaction becomes the only exit — a game with no visible link back leaves the user stuck.

claim: Always give the 404 an automatic or obvious route back into the product; the playful element is a wrapper around the redirect, not a replacement for it.
why: The referenced pizza site redirects the moment the game is completed, so the delight resolves into navigation instead of dead-ending.
when: Any interactive or unconventional error page.

claim: Write error-page copy in the same voice as the rest of the site's microcopy so the personality reads as one consistent character rather than a one-off gag.
why: The demo's 404 deliberately carries over the personal writing tone set up earlier in the project, which is what makes it feel bespoke instead of borrowed.
when: When you have already established a distinct copy voice elsewhere in the product.
fails: On a product with an otherwise neutral, institutional voice, where a suddenly chatty 404 feels like a different team wrote it.

claim: Pair the error page's visual joke with a short, smooth entrance animation instead of leaving elements static.
why: Motion is what makes a simple, low-element page feel finished and intentional rather than unstyled.
when: Sparse pages with few components, where there is little else carrying the sense of craft.
fails: When the animation delays the user seeing the way back to a working page.

claim: Budget your personality for the low-stakes, low-traffic screens — 404s, empty states, loading states — and keep the primary task flows plain.
why: This is the closing argument of the whole piece: the difference between corporate-generic and bespoke lives in the details nobody was required to design, not in the core flows.
when: Working within a restrained brand or a functional product where the main flows can't carry decoration.
fails: When it becomes an excuse to leave the primary experience undesigned — the detail layer is additive, not a substitute for the core work.

claim: Add delayed hover tooltips to unlabeled icons when persistent text labels would overcrowd the interface.
why: They make compact controls understandable while keeping the main layout visually economical.
when: An interface contains icons whose meanings may not be immediately obvious and available space is limited.
fails: null

claim: Only reveal a hover tooltip after the pointer remains over its trigger for about one second.
why: The delay filters out accidental or passing hovers, so the interface does not produce distracting popups.
when: Tooltips are triggered by pointer hover over controls or icons.
fails: null

claim: Implement tooltip visibility with separate pointer-enter and pointer-leave states, returning to the base state immediately when the pointer exits.
why: The tooltip should appear conditionally during intentional inspection and disappear once its trigger is no longer active.
when: Prototyping or building hover-driven desktop interactions.
fails: null

claim: Use a restrained custom easing curve on tooltip entrance when a subtle bounce supports the product’s motion style.
why: A tailored easing curve can make the reveal feel more responsive and polished than a default transition.
when: The interface benefits from expressive but lightweight microinteraction motion.
fails: Overly bouncy motion can make utility feedback feel distracting or slow.
